sections.label: Markets & Macro
sections.title: Inflation ran hot, and gold took the hit
paragraphs: US consumer prices, published on 14 October, came in warmer than forecast. The dollar and bond yields jumped, and gold dropped about 1.5% that day to roughly $4,100–4,150 an ounce. It is now down around 4% this year. The Fed meets on 27–28 October and markets mostly expect it to sit still.
Why gold hates this news: hot inflation means rates stay high for longer. Gold pays no interest, so when your cash and bonds pay you more, holding it looks less clever.

why.head: Why it matters
why.text: Inflation decides interest rates, and interest rates quietly decide almost everything else: mortgages, savings, stock prices and what your euros buy abroad.

sections.label: AI Build
sections.title: Snap a receipt, get a monthly spending report
paragraphs: The idea: you take a photo of every receipt. AI reads it, pulls out the date, shop, amount and category, and adds a row to a spreadsheet. At the end of the month it writes you a short summary.
bullets: Simplest: a Claude Project called "Receipts". Drop photos in, ask for a table.
Automated: ask Claude Code for a script that sends each photo to Claude and appends to a Google Sheet.
Monthly report: a scheduled task that emails you the summary on the 1st.

why.head: Could you sell it?
why.text: The general version exists (Expensify, Dext). The money is in a niche, like Airbnb hosts or tradespeople in one country with local VAT rules. <mark>Narrow tools are easier to sell than broad ones.</mark>

sections.label: Art & Collecting
sections.title: Provenance: an object's paper trail
paragraphs: Provenance is the recorded history of who has owned a work, from the artist's studio until today. <mark>A solid provenance does two jobs: it helps prove the work is genuine, and it shows nobody has a claim to get it back.</mark>
Gaps make buyers nervous, especially for Europe between 1933 and 1945, when the Nazis looted huge amounts of art.

why.head: Why it matters
why.text: When a catalogue says "impeccable provenance," it means: we know exactly where this has been, and nobody will come knocking for it.

sections.label: Philosophy
sections.quote: We suffer more often in imagination than in reality.
sections.cite: Seneca, Letters to Lucilius, XIII · c. 65 AD
paragraphs: Seneca was one of the richest men in Rome and worked for Nero, so he had a lot to worry about. His advice to a younger friend: <mark>separate what is happening from what you fear might happen, and only deal with the first.</mark>

sections.title: Thinking, Fast and Slow, by Daniel Kahneman
paragraphs: A Nobel-winning psychologist explains the two "systems" in your head: <mark>a fast one that runs on instinct and shortcuts, and a slow one that does careful thinking but is lazy.</mark>
